summary: Provides a road map of the LDAP technical specification, a set of documents on accessing distributed directory services built on X.500 data and service models. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A table of contents that says which documents in the LDAP series to read for each topic.

subtitle: The table of contents for LDAP version 3: which documents together make up the technical specification.

tldr.problem: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol was spread over many documents that had grown up piecemeal, and the older road map no longer matched them.
tldr.mechanism: This document names the nine documents that, together with itself, form the LDAP version 3 technical specification, and states how the suite relates to X.500 and to the specifications it replaces.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3377 and nine other RFCs (2251 to 2256, 2829, 2830 and 3771) and redefines the terms LDAP and LDAPv3 to mean this revised suite.

facts.label: Documents in the suite
facts.value: This road map plus nine others

today: RFC 4510 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It replaces RFC 3377 and the other RFCs it obsoletes.

sections.title: The LDAP Technical Specification
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an Internet protocol for accessing distributed directory services that act in accordance with X.500 data and service models. RFC 4510 is a road map. It does not define the protocol itself, but lists the documents that do.

The technical specification for LDAP version 3 consists of this document and nine others: the protocol (RFC 4511), directory information models (RFC 4512), authentication methods and security mechanisms (RFC 4513), string representation of distinguished names (RFC 4514), string representation of search filters (RFC 4515), the LDAP URL (RFC 4516), syntaxes and matching rules (RFC 4517), internationalized string preparation (RFC 4518) and the schema for user applications (RFC 4519).

The terms "LDAP" and "LDAPv3" are used informally for the protocol this specification defines. Other documents should identify the LDAP suite formally by a normative reference to RFC 4510.
sections.eli5: LDAP is like a big phone book that many computers can look things up in. This document is the list of all the instruction booklets that explain how the phone book works.

sections.title: The Companion Documents
sections.content:
Each document in the suite covers one slice of LDAP. The protocol itself, with its message exchanges, is in RFC 4511. The data it works on, the directory information models, are in RFC 4512, and the schema for common user applications is in RFC 4519.

Names and queries have their own documents: RFC 4514 for distinguished names as strings, RFC 4515 for search filters as strings, and RFC 4516 for the LDAP Uniform Resource Locator. Syntaxes and matching rules are in RFC 4517, and RFC 4518 covers internationalized string preparation. Security is in RFC 4513.

Of these, only RFC 4518 is new to this revision. The rest rework earlier documents.
sections.eli5: One booklet explains how to ask the phone book a question, another how names are written, another how to keep it safe. Together they make the whole set.

sections.title: Relationship to X.500
sections.content:
The specification defines LDAP in terms of X.500 as an access mechanism. An LDAP server MUST act in accordance with the X.500 (1993) series of ITU-T Recommendations when providing the service.

It is not required that a server use any X.500 protocols to do so. LDAP can be mapped onto any other directory system, as long as the X.500 data and service models (X.501 and X.511), as used in LDAP, are not violated at the LDAP interface.

The specification explicitly incorporates portions of X.500(93). Later revisions of X.500 do not automatically apply to it.
sections.eli5: LDAP has to play by the same rules as an older, bigger directory system. But the computer behind it can be built any way, as long as it acts the same from outside.

sections.title: Relationship to Obsolete Specifications
sections.content:
This specification obsoletes entirely the previous LDAP technical specification defined in RFC 3377, which consisted of RFCs 2251 to 2256, 2829, 2830, 3771 and RFC 3377 itself. The suite was significantly reorganized.

RFC 4510 replaces RFC 3377 and Section 3.3 of RFC 2251. Appendix A.1 says it is nearly a complete rewrite of RFC 3377 because much of that material no longer applied, and that it redefines "LDAP" and "LDAPv3" to refer to this revision. Appendix A.2 notes that Section 3.3 of RFC 2251 changed slightly: the word "document" became "technical specification", to show it applies to the entire suite.

Each document in the suite has appendices summarizing the changes to the sections of the specifications it replaces. Portions of the suite may also update or replace other documents, and these relationships are described in the documents concerned.
sections.eli5: This is a new edition of the instruction set. The old booklets were shuffled around and replaced, so the new list says which new booklet took over from which old one.

sections.title: Extensions and IANA
sections.content:
LDAP is an extensible protocol. Extensions may be specified in other documents, and they are expected to be truly optional. The considerations for LDAP extensions in BCP 118, RFC 4521, apply fully to this revision.

Nomenclature for LDAP-plus-extensions combinations is not defined here, though a future document may define it. The IANA considerations in BCP 64, RFC 4520, also apply fully.
sections.eli5: You can add extra features to LDAP, but they have to be optional, so that everyone can still talk to each other even if they skip them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4510 adds no security text of its own. It states only that LDAP security considerations are discussed in each document that makes up the technical specification.

The authentication methods and security mechanisms are specified in RFC 4513, so that is the natural starting point for security questions.
sections.eli5: Each booklet has its own safety section, so this list just points you to them.
